entries.49932b1c8fc7da3319429bc83a4d89e47215a04a: <div sID="gen8162" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="15" osisID="2Chr.15" sID="2Chr.15"/> <div eID="gen8162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8163" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8164" type="x-p"/> Asa and his army were now returning in triumph from the battle, laden with spoils and adorned with the trophies of victory, the pious prince, we may now suppose, studying what he should render to God for this great favour. He knew that the work of reformation, which he had begun in his kingdom, was not perfected; his enemies abroad were subdued, but there were more dangerous enemies at home that were yet unconquered—idols in Judah and Benjamin: his victory over the former emboldened him vigorously to renew his attack upon the latter. Now here we have, I. The message which God sent to him, by a prophet, to engage him to, and encourage him in, the prosecution of his reformation, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1-2Chr.15.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. The life which this message put into that good cause, and their proceedings in pursuance of it. Idols removed, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">ver. 8</reference>. The spoil dedicated to God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.9-2Chr.15.11">ver. 9-11</reference>. A covenant made with God, and a law for the punishing of idolaters, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.12-2Chr.15.15">ver. 12-15</reference>. A reformation at court, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">ver. 16</reference>. Dedicated things brought into the house of God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.18">ver. 18</reference>. All well, but that the high places were permitted, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.17">ver. 17</reference>. And the effect of this was great peace, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">ver. 19</reference>.
entries.2ce7e560606ba505182265ce7e85e119502ba567: <div eID="gen8164" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8163" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Message to Asa. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 945.)</title> <div sID="gen8165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And the Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: <hi type="super">2</hi> And he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now for a long season Israel <hi type="italic">hath been</hi> without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law. <hi type="super">4</hi> But when they in their trouble did turn unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, and sought him, he was found of them. <hi type="super">5</hi> And in those times <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no peace to him that went out, nor to him that came in, but great vexations <hi type="italic">were</hi> upon all the inhabitants of the countries. <hi type="super">6</hi> And nation was destroyed of nation, and city of city: for God did vex them with all adversity. <hi type="super">7</hi> Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded. <div eID="gen8165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8166" type="x-p"/> It was a great happiness to Israel that they had prophets among them; yet, while they were thus blessed, they were strangely addicted to idolatry, whereas, when the spirit of prophecy had ceased under the second temple, and the canon of the Old Temple was completed (which was constantly read in their synagogues), they were pure from idolatry; for the scriptures are of all other the <hi type="italic">most sure word of prophecy,</hi> and most effectual, and the church could not be so easily imposed upon by a counterfeit Bible as by a counterfeit prophet. Here was a prophet sent to Asa and his army, when they returned victorious from the war with the Ethiopians, not to compliment them and congratulate them on their success, but to quicken them to their duty; this is the proper business of God's ministers, even with princes and the greatest men. The <hi type="italic">Spirit of God came</hi> upon the prophet (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1">v. 1</reference>), both to instruct him what he should say and to enable him to say it with clearness and boldness. <div eID="gen8166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8167" type="x-p"/> I. He told them plainly upon what terms they stood with God. Let them not think that, having obtained this victory, all was their own for ever; no, he must let them know they were upon their good behaviour. Let them do well, and it will be well with them, otherwise not. 1. <hi type="italic">The Lord is with you while you are with him.</hi> This is both a word of comfort, that those who keep close to God shall always have his presence with them, and also a word of caution: "He is <hi type="italic">with you, while you are with him,</hi> but no longer; you have now a signal token of his favourable presence with you, but the continuance of it depends upon your perseverance in the way of your duty." 2. "<hi type="italic">If you seek him, he will be found of you.</hi> Sincerely desire his favour, and aim at it, and you shall obtain it. Pray, and you shall prevail. He never said, nor ever will, <hi type="italic">Seek you me in vain.</hi>" See <reference osisRef="Heb.11.6">Heb. xi. 6</reference>. But, 3. "If you forsake him and his ordinances, he is not tied to you, but will certainly forsake you, and then you are undone, your present triumphs will be no security to you; woe to you when God departs." <div eID="gen8167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8168" type="x-p"/> II. He set before them the dangerous consequence of forsaking God and his ordinances, and that there was no way of having grievances redressed, but by repenting, and returning unto God. When Israel forsook their duty they were over-run with a deluge of atheism, impiety, irreligion, and all irregularity (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">v. 3</reference>), and were continually embarrassed with vexatious and destroying wars, foreign and domestic, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5-2Chr.15.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. But when their troubles drove them to God they found it not in vain to seek him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.4">v. 4</reference>. But the question is, What time does this refer to? 1. Some think it looks as far back as the days of the Judges. <hi type="italic">A long season</hi> ago Israel was <hi type="italic">without the true God,</hi> for they worshipped false gods; it was a time of ignorance, for, though they had priests, they had no teaching priests, though they had elders, yet no law to any purpose, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">v. 3</reference>. These were sad times, when they were frequently oppressed by one enemy or other and grievously harassed by Moabites, Midianites, Ammonites, and other nations. They were <hi type="italic">vexed with all adversity</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.6">v. 6</reference>), yet when, in their perplexity, they turned to God by repentance, prayer, and reformation, he raised up deliverers for them. Then was that maxim often verified, that God is with us while we are with him. Whatsoever things of this kind were written aforetime were written for our admonition. 2. Others think it describes the state of the ten tribes (who were now properly called <hi type="italic">Israel</hi>) in the days of Asa. "<hi type="italic">Now,</hi> since Jeroboam set up the calves, though he pretended to honour the God that brought them out of Egypt, yet his idolatry has brought them to downright infidelity; they are <hi type="italic">without the true God,</hi>" and no marvel when they were without teaching priests. Jeroboam's priests were not teachers, and thus they came to be without law. It is next to impossible that any thing of religion should be kept up without a preaching ministry. In those times there was no peace, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">v. 5</reference>. Their war with Judah gave them frequent alarms; so did the late insurrection of Baasha and other occasions not mentioned. They provoked God with all iniquity, and then he <hi type="italic">vexed them with all adversity;</hi> yet, <hi type="italic">when they turned to God,</hi> he was entreated for them. Let Judah take notice of this; let their neighbours' harms be their warnings. Give no countenance to graven images for you see what mischiefs they produce. 3. Others think the whole passage may be read in the future tense, and that it looks forward: Hereafter <hi type="italic">Israel will be without the true God and a teaching priest,</hi> and they will be destroyed by one judgment after another till they <hi type="italic">return to God</hi> and <hi type="italic">seek him.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Hos.3.4">Hos. iii. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen8168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8169" type="x-p"/> III. Upon this he grounded his exhortation to prosecute the work of reformation with vigour (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be strong, for your work shall be rewarded.</hi> Note, 1. God's work should be done with diligence and cheerfulness, but will not be done without resolution. 2. This should quicken us to the work of religion, that we shall be sure not to lose by it ultimately. It will not go unrewarded. How should it, when the work is its own reward?
entries.906fdad3adc0f4bf6569d124d644518bfaef799c: <div eID="gen8169" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Asa Reforms His Kingdom. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 940.)</title> <div sID="gen8170" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And when Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from mount Ephraim, and renewed the altar of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , that <hi type="italic">was</hi> before the porch of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> And he gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh, and out of Simeon: for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance, when they saw that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God <hi type="italic">was</hi> with him. <hi type="super">10</hi> So they gathered themselves together at Jerusalem in the third month, in the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they offered unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> the same time, of the spoil <hi type="italic">which</hi> they had brought, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep. <hi type="super">12</hi> And they entered into a covenant to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul; <hi type="super">13</hi> That whosoever would not seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman. <hi type="super">14</hi> And they sware unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets. <hi type="super">15</hi> And all Judah rejoiced at the oath: for they had sworn with all their heart, and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found of them: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> gave them rest round about. <hi type="super">16</hi> And also <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> Maachah the mother of Asa the king, he removed her from <hi type="italic">being</hi> queen, because she had made an idol in a grove: and Asa cut down her idol, and stamped <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and burnt <hi type="italic">it</hi> at the brook Kidron. <hi type="super">17</hi> But the high places were not taken away out of Israel: nevertheless the heart of Asa was perfect all his days. <hi type="super">18</hi> And he brought into the house of God the things that his father had dedicated, and that he himself had dedicated, silver, and gold, and vessels. <hi type="super">19</hi> And there was no <hi type="italic">more</hi> war unto the five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa. <div eID="gen8170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8171" type="x-p"/> We are here told what good effect the foregoing sermon had upon Asa. <div eID="gen8171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8172" type="x-p"/> I. He grew more bold for God than he had been. His victory would inspire him with some new degrees of resolution, but this message from God with much more. Now he took courage. He saw how necessary a further reformation was, and what assurance he had of God's presence with him in it; and this made him daring, and helped him over the difficulties which had before deterred him and driven him off from the undertaking. Now he ventured to destroy all the abominable idols (and all idolatries are abominable, <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1 Pet. iv. 3</reference>) as far as ever his power went. Away with them all. He also <hi type="italic">renewed the altar of the Lord,</hi> which, it seems, had gone out of repair, though it was not above thirty-five years since Solomon's head was laid, who erected it. So soon did these ceremonial institutions begin to wax old, as things which, in the fulness of time, must <hi type="italic">vanish away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.8.13">Heb. viii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen8172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8173" type="x-p"/> II. He extended his influence further than before, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.9">v. 9</reference>. He summoned a solemn assembly, and particularly brought the strangers to it, who had come over to him from the ten tribes. 1. Their coming was a great encouragement to him; for the reason of their coming was because <hi type="italic">they saw that the Lord his God was with him.</hi> It is good to be with those that have God with them, to come into relation to, and contract acquaintance and friendship with, those that live in the fear and favour of God. <hi type="italic">We will go with you, for we have heard that God is with you,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.8.23">Zech. viii. 23</reference>. 2. The cognizance he took of them, and the invitation he gave them to the general assembly, were a great encouragement to them. All strangers are to be helped, but those that cast themselves upon God's good providence, purely to keep a good conscience, are worthy of double honour. Asa gave orders for the gathering of them together (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.9">v. 9</reference>), yet it is said (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">v. 10</reference>) that they <hi type="italic">gathered themselves together,</hi> made it their own act, so forward were they to obey the king's orders. This meeting was held in the third month, probably at the feast of Pentecost, which was in that month. <div eID="gen8173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8174" type="x-p"/> III. He and his people offered sacrifices to God, as his share of the spoil they had got, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.11">v. 11</reference>. Their offering here was nothing to Solomon's (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.5">ch. vii. 5</reference>), which was owing to the diminution either of their zeal or of their wealth, or of both. These sacrifices were intended by way of thanksgiving for the favours they had received, and supplication for further favours. Prayers and praises are now our spiritual sacrifices. And, as he took care that the altar should have its gift, so he took care that the temple should have its gold: <hi type="italic">He brought into the house of God all the dedicated things,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.18">v. 18</reference>. It is honesty to render to God the things that are his. What has been long designed for him, and long laid by for him, as it should seem these dedicated things had been, should at length be laid out for him. Will a man rob God, or make slow payment to him, who is always ready to do us good? <div eID="gen8174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8175" type="x-p"/> IV. <hi type="italic">They entered into covenant with God,</hi> repenting that they had violated their engagements to him and resolving to do better for the future. It is proper for penitents, for converts, to renew their covenants. It should seem, the motion came not from Asa, but from the people themselves. Let every man be a volunteer that covenants with God. <hi type="italic">Thy people shall be willing,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen8175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8176" type="x-p"/> 1. What was the matter of this covenant. Nothing but what they were before obliged to; and, though no vow or promise of theirs could lay any higher obligation upon them than they were already under from the divine precept, yet it would help to increase their sense of the obligation, to arm them against temptations, and would be a testimony to the equity and goodness of the precept. And, by joining all together in this covenant, they strengthened the hands one of another. Two things they engaged themselves to:—(1.) That they would diligently seek God themselves, seek his precepts, seek his favour. What is religion but seeking God, enquiring after him, applying to him, upon all occasions? We shall not enjoy him till we come to heaven; while we are here we must continue seeking. They would seek God as the <hi type="italic">God of their fathers,</hi> in the way that their fathers sought him and in dependence upon the promise made to their fathers; and they would do it <hi type="italic">with all their heart</hi> and <hi type="italic">with all their soul,</hi> for those only seek God acceptably and successfully that are inward with him, intent upon him, and entire for him, in their seeking him. We make nothing of our religion if we do not make heart-work of it. God will have all the heart or none; and, when a jewel of such inestimable value as the divine favour is to be found, it is worth while to seek it <hi type="italic">with all our soul.</hi> (2.) That they would, to the utmost of their power, oblige others to seek him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.13">v. 13</reference>. They agreed that <hi type="italic">whosoever would not seek the Lord God of Israel</hi> (that is, would either worship other gods or refuse to join with them in the worship of the true God, that was either an obstinate idolater or an obstinate atheist) he should be put to death. This was no new law of their own making, but an order to put in execution that law of God to this purport, <reference osisRef="Deut.17.2-Deut.17.5">Deut. xvii. 2</reference>, &c. If this law had been duly executed, there would not have been so many abominable idols found in Judah and Benjamin, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">v. 8</reference>. Whether men may now, under the gospel, be compelled by such methods as these to seek the Lord is justly questioned; for the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, and yet mighty. <div eID="gen8176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8177" type="x-p"/> 2. In what manner they made this covenant. (1.) With great cheerfulness, and all possible expressions of joy: <hi type="italic">The swore unto the Lord;</hi> not secretly, as if they were either ashamed of what they did or afraid of binding themselves too fast to him, but with a loud voice, to express their own zeal and to animate one another; and they all rejoiced at the oath, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.14-2Chr.15.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. They did not swear to God with reluctancy (as the poor debtor confesses a judgment to his creditor), but with all the pleasure and satisfaction imaginable, as the bridegroom plights his troth to the bride in the marriage covenant. Every honest Israelite was pleased with his own engagements to God, and they were all pleased with one another's. They rejoiced in it as a hopeful expedient to prevent their apostasy from God and a happy indication of God's presence with them. Note, The times of renewing our covenant with God should be times of rejoicing, and national reformation cannot but give general satisfaction to all that are good. It is an honour and happiness to be in bonds to God. (2.) They did it with great sincerity, zeal and resolution: <hi type="italic">They swore to God with all their hearts,</hi> and <hi type="italic">sought him with their whole desire.</hi> The Israelites were now in an extraordinarily good frame. O that there had always been such a heart in them! This comes in as the reason why they rejoiced so much in what they did: it was because they were hearty in it. Note, Those only experience the pleasure and comfort of religion that are sincere and upright in it. What is done in hypocrisy is a mere drudgery. But, if God has the heart, we have the joy. <div eID="gen8177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8178" type="x-p"/> V. We are told what was the effect of this their solemn covenanting with God. 1. God did well for them: <hi type="italic">He</hi> was <hi type="italic">found of them, and gave them rest round about</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.15">v. 15</reference>), so that there was no war for a long time after (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">v. 19</reference>), no open general war, though there were constant bickerings between Judah and Israel upon the frontiers, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16">1 Kings xv. 16</reference>. National piety procures national blessings. 2. They did, on the whole, well for him. They carried on the reformation so far that Maachah the queen-mother was deposed for idolatry and her idol destroyed, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">v. 16</reference>. This was bravely done of Asa, that he would not connive at idolatry in those that were nearest to him, like Levi, that <hi type="italic">said to his father and mother, I have not seen him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. Asa knows he must honour God more than his grandmother, and dares not leave an idol in an apartment of his palace while he is destroying idols in the cities of his kingdom. We may suppose this Maachah was so far convinced of her sin that she was willing to subscribe the association mentioned (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.12-2Chr.15.13">v. 12, 13</reference>), binding herself to seek the Lord, and therefore was not put to death as those were that refused to sign it, great as well as small, women as well as men: probably it was with an eye to her that <hi type="italic">women</hi> were specified. But because she had been an idolater Asa thought fit to divest her of the dignity and authority she had, and probably he banished her the court and confined her to privacy, lest she should influence and infect others. But the reformation was not complete; the high places were not all taken away, though many of them were, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">ch. xiv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">5</reference>. Those in the cities were removed, but not those in the cities of Judah, but not those in the cities of Israel which were reduced to the house of David; or those that were used in the service of false gods, but not those that were used in the service of the God of Israel. These he connived at, and yet his heart was perfect. There may be defects in some particular duties where yet the heart, in the man, is upright with God. Sincerity is something less than sinless perfection.  <chapter eID="2Chr.15"/> <div eID="gen8178" type="x-p"/>

entries.8b977205fd23131558e9fcf56759b459ff2bb089: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4016"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 15</title> <div sID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1-2Chr.15.15">2Ch 15:1-15</reference>. Judah Makes a Solemn Covenant with God.<div eID="gen5807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4016"/><hi type="bold">1. Azariah the son of Oded--</hi>This prophet, who is mentioned nowhere else, appears at this stage of the sacred story in the discharge of an interesting mission. He went to meet Asa, as he was returning from his victorious pursuit of the Ethiopians, and the congratulatory address here recorded was publicly made to the king in presence of his army. <div eID="gen5808" type="x-p"/>
entries.fb992695515a9fa781618dd53bef0382056ebf0d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4017"/><div sID="gen5809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4017"/><hi type="bold">2. The Lord is with you, while ye be with him--</hi>You have had, in your recent signal success, a remarkable proof that God's blessing is upon you; your victory has been the reward of your faith and piety. If you steadfastly adhere to the cause of God, you may expect a continuance of His favor; but if you abandon it, you will soon reap the bitter fruits of apostasy. <div eID="gen5809" type="x-p"/>
entries.2870f5d7fab182b15fac452fab90ef5bcd167652: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4018"/><div sID="gen5810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4018"/><hi type="bold">3-6. Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, &c.--</hi>Some think that Azariah was referring to the sad and disastrous condition to which superstition and idolatry had brought the neighboring kingdom of Israel. His words should rather be taken in a wider sense, for it seems manifest that the prophet had his eye upon many periods in the national history, when the people were in the state described--a state of spiritual destitution and ignorance--and exhibited its natural result as widespread anarchy, mutual dissension among the tribes, and general suffering (<reference osisRef="Judg.9.23">Jud 9:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.12.4">12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Judg.20.21">20:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.17">2Ch 13:17</reference>). These calamities God permitted to befall them as the punishment of their apostasy. Azariah's object in these remarks was to establish the truth of his counsel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.2">2Ch 15:2</reference>), threatening, in case of neglecting it by describing the uniform course of the divine procedure towards Israel, as shown in all periods of their history. Then after this appeal to national experience, he concluded with an earnest exhortation to the king to prosecute the work of reformation so well begun [2Ch 15:7]. <div eID="gen5810" type="x-p"/>
entries.ae11c87ccaf69aa3e29c3f4cc519491aae4f83b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4019"/><div sID="gen5811" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4019"/><hi type="bold">7. Be ye strong--</hi>Great resolution and indomitable energy would be required to persevere in the face of the opposition your reforming measures will encounter.<div eID="gen5811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5812" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">your work shall be rewarded--</hi>What you do in the cause and for the glory of God will assuredly be followed by the happiest results both to yourself and your subjects. <div eID="gen5812" type="x-p"/>
entries.28a1d6e3db0adda2cae8b57784d6bd29c8aa1715: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4020"/><div sID="gen5813" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4020"/><hi type="bold">8. when Asa heard ... the prophecy of Oded the prophet--</hi>The insertion of these words, "of Oded the prophet," is generally regarded as a corruption of the text. "The sole remedy is to erase them. They are, probably, the remains of a note, which crept in from the margin into the text" [Bertheau].<div eID="gen5813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5814" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he took courage--</hi>Animated by the seasonable and pious address of Azariah, Asa became a more zealous reformer than ever, employing all his royal authority and influence to extirpate every vestige of idolatry from the land.<div eID="gen5814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5815" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and out of the cities which he had taken from mount Ephraim--</hi>He may have acquired cities of Ephraim, the conquest of which is not recorded (<reference osisRef="2Chr.17.2">2Ch 17:2</reference>); but it has been commonly supposed that the reference is to cities which his father Abijah had taken in that quarter (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>).<div eID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5816" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">renewed the altar of the Lord ... before the porch--</hi>that is, the altar of burnt offering. As this was done on or about the fifteenth year of the reign of this pious king, the renewal must have consisted in some splendid repairs or embellishments, which made it look like a new dedication, or in a reconstruction of a temporary altar, like that of Solomon (<reference osisRef="2Chr.7.7">2Ch 7:7</reference>), for extraordinary sacrifices to be offered on an approaching occasion. <div eID="gen5816" type="x-p"/>
entries.8533f46d008edb8760f60b5f3bbc67a2a9838e26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4021"/><div sID="gen5817" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4021"/><hi type="bold">9-15. he gathered all Judah and Benjamin--</hi>Not satisfied with these minor measures of purification and improvement, Asa meditated a grand scheme which was to pledge his whole kingdom to complete the work of reformation, and with this in view he waited for a general assembly of the people.<div eID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5818" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the strangers with them out of Ephraim and Manasseh--</hi>The population of Asa's kingdom had been vastly increased by the continued influx of strangers, who, prompted by motives either of interest or of piety, sought in his dominions that security and freedom which they could not enjoy amid the complicated troubles which distracted Israel.<div eID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5819" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and out of Simeon--</hi>Although a portion of that tribe, located within the territory of Judah, were already subjects of the southern kingdom, the general body of the Simeonites had joined in forming the northern kingdom of Israel. But many of them now returned of their own accord. <div eID="gen5819" type="x-p"/>
entries.132ab6ac68748c54df817f53f24db7aa68049562: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4023"/><div sID="gen5821" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4023"/><hi type="bold">18. the things that his father had dedicated--</hi>probably part of the booty obtained by his signal victory over Jeroboam, but which, though dedicated, had hitherto been unrepresented.<div eID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5822" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and that he himself had dedicated--</hi>of the booty taken from the Ethiopians. Both of these were now deposited in the temple as votive offerings to Him whose right hand and holy arm had given them the victory. <chapter eID="2Chr.15"/>

entries.6d62c56057f68c5d52e5c9eabe528afe2e62f15c: <div eID="gen14226" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14227" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14228" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14227" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> Azariah's prophecy concerning Israel, and his exhortation to Asa, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1-2Chr.15.7">2Chr 15:1-7</reference>. Asa completes the reformation which he had begun, his kingdom is greatly strengthened, and all to people make a solemn covenant with the Lord, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8-2Chr.15.15">2Chr 15:8-15</reference>. His treatment of his mother Maachah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Chr 15:16</reference>. He brings into the house of God the things that has father had dedicated, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.17">2Chr 15:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.18">2Chr 15:18</reference>. And he has no war till the thirty-fifth year of his reign, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Chr 15:19</reference>. <div eID="gen14229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen14230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> Azariah the son of Oded - We know nothing of this prophet but what is related of him here.
entries.da8209775f7406e2b69db12fc268490a904bdb9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> The Lord is with you, while ye be with him - This is the settled and eternal purpose of God; to them who seek him he will ever be found propitious, and them alone will he abandon who forsake him. In this verse the unconditional perseverance of the saints has no place: a doctrine which was first the ruin of the human race, Ye shall not die; and ever since the fall, has been the plague and disgrace of the Church of Christ. The Targum is curious: "Hearken to me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: The Word of the Lord shall be your helper, while ye walk in his ways. If ye seek doctrine from his presence he will be found of you in times of trouble; but if you cast away his fear, he will abandon you."
entries.c71289f897c52d041d69832055b11dbef0c47b3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> Now for a long season Israel - "Israel hath followed Jeroboam, and they have not worshipped the true God. They have burnt incense to their golden calves; their priestlings [כומריא cumeraiya, their black, sooty sacrificers] have burnt perfumes with a strange worship, and have not exercised themselves in the law." - Targum. These priests could not teach, because they had not learnt; and as they had abandoned the law of the Lord, consequently they had no proper matter for instruction. <div eID="gen14233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> There is a great diversity of opinions concerning the meaning of this text. Some consider it a prophecy relative to the future state of this people, and the final destruction of the Jews as to their political existence: others consider it as referring to the state of the people under the reigns of Rehoboam and Abijah, which were happily changed under that of Asa; and this appears to me to be the most natural sense of the words.
entries.4657ebc9b6ac0bdf772c7e005e2e8f3f3c4ae6aa: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> But great vexations - Does not our Lord allude to this and the following verse in <reference osisRef="Mat.24.6">Mat 24:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.7">Mat 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.9">Mat 24:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.24.13">Mat 24:13</reference>?
entries.5360717703bfd82d3448497677bc8c6c65147c5b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen14235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> Renewed the altar - Dedicated it afresh, or perhaps enlarged it, that more sacrifices might be offered on it than ever before; for it cannot be supposed that this altar had no victims offered on it till the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa, who had previously been so zealous in restoring the Divine worship.
entries.4cfaa6d8d295db1294b7c4c1a43c0ac6e1201db4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> And the strangers - Many out of the different tribes, particularly out of Simeon, Ephraim, and Manasseh, having reflected that the Divine blessing was promised to the house of David, and finding the government of Jeroboam founded in idolatry, would naturally, through a spirit of piety, leave their own country, and go where they might enjoy the worship of the true God.
entries.d166b8a08bfbe1f48990ae3b88c8e6119603c6d9: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> The third month - At the feast of pentecost which was held on the third month.
entries.395fea6efa09669ac20277e43afff05cfc176446: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen14238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> The spoil which they had brought - The spoil which they had taken from Zerah and his auxiliaries, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14">2Chr 14:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.15">2Chr 14:15</reference>.
entries.ea15f231dbb1b0fbe44ca4ead27cc6f1de1b7c67: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> They entered into a covenant - The covenant consisted of two parts: <div eID="gen14240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> 1. We will seek the God of our fathers with all our heart, and with all our soul. <div eID="gen14241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> 2. Whosoever, great or small, man or woman, will not worship the true God, and serve him alone, shall be put to death. Thus no toleration was given to idolatry, so that it must be rooted out: and that this covenant might be properly binding, they confirmed it with an oath; and God accepted them and their services.
entries.9a90aa8d3ab48bee487cae54c05419cc60b8f712: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen14242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> Concerning Maachah - See the matter fully explained in the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">1Kgs 15:13</reference> (note). <div eID="gen14243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> The Jews imagine that Maachah repented, and her name became changed into Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah; and that this was done that there might be no mention of her former name, lest it should be a reproach to her: but we have already seen another gloss on this name. See on <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">2Chr 11:20</reference> (note).
entries.4189a44b59f45182c0e6a6fa00902f228b859e64: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen14244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14245" type="x-p"/> The high places were not taken away - He had totally suppressed or destroyed the idolatry; but some of the places, buildings, or altars, he permitted to remain.
entries.f98fcd1049caef657028606a90367473e9ddd80b: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14246" type="x-p"/> The things that his father had dedicated - As it was a custom to dedicate a part of the spoils taken from an enemy to the service and honor of God, it is natural to suppose that Abijah, having so signally overthrown Jeroboam, (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.15-2Chr.13.19">2Chr 13:15-19</reference>), had dedicated a part of the spoils to the Lord; but they had not been brought into the temple till this time. <div eID="gen14246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14247" type="x-p"/> Silver, and gold, and vessels - The word כלים kelim, which we translate vessels, signifies instruments, utensils, ornaments, etc.
entries.ff13335448e2dbc5f17f6696e2f96a25336707a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen14247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14248" type="x-p"/> The five and thirtieth year of the reign of Asa - Archbishop Usher thinks that this should be counted from the separation of the kingdom, and that this fell on the fifteenth year of Asa's reign. To settle in every respect these chronologies is a most difficult undertaking; and the difficulty does not belong to the sacred books alone, all other chronological tables of all the nations in the world, are in the same predicament. With those of our own history I have often been puzzled, even while I had access to all the archives of the nation. Probably we should read here the five and twentieth year. See the note on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.16">1Kgs 15:16</reference>.  <chapter eID="2Chr.15"/> <div eID="gen14248" type="x-p"/>

entries.09b8bd26e48daa83d32099945ef2cfb0e90b902b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1-2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:1-4</reference> <hi type="italic">The prophet Azariah’s exhortation to faithful cleaving to the Lord, and the solemn renewal of the covenant</hi>. - <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1">2Ch 15:1</reference>-7. The prophet’s speech. The prophet Azariah, the son of Oded, is mentioned only here. The conjecture of some of the older theologians, that עודד was the same person as עדּו   (<reference osisRef="2Chr.12.15">2Ch 12:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Ch 9:29</reference>), has no tenable foundation. Azariah went to meet the king and people returning from the war (לפני יצא, he went forth in the presence of Asa, i.e., coming before him; cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.9">2Ch 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.17">1Ch 12:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.8">1Ch 14:8</reference>). “Jahve was with you (has given you the victory), because ye were with Him (held to Him).” Hence the general lesson is drawn: If ye seek Him, He will be found of you (cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.29.13">Jer 29:13</reference>); and if ye forsake Him, He will forsake you (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.24.20">2Ch 24:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.5">2Ch 12:5</reference>). To impress the people deeply with this truth, Azariah draws a powerful picture of the times when a people is forsaken by God, when peace and security in social intercourse disappear, and the terrors of civil war prevail. Opinions as to the reference intended in this portrayal of the dreadful results of defection from God have been from antiquity very much divided. Tremell. and Grot., following the Targ., take the words to refer to the condition of the kingdom of the ten tribes at that time; others think they refer to the past, either to the immediately preceding period of the kingdom of Judah, to the times of the defection under Rehoboam and Abijah, before Asa had suppressed idolatry (Syr., Arab., Raschi), or to the more distant past, the anarchic period of the judges, from Joshua’s death, and that of the high priest Phinehas, until Eli and Samuel’s reformation (so especially Vitringa, <hi type="italic">de synag. vet.</hi> p. 335ff.). Finally, still others (Luther, Clericus, Budd., etc.) interpret the words as prophetic, as descriptive of the future, and make them refer either to the unquiet times under the later idolatrous kings, to the times of the Assyrian or Chaldean exile (Kimchi), or to the condition of the Jews since the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans up till the present day. Of these three views, the first, that which takes the reference to be to the present, i.e., the state of the kingdom of the ten tribes at that time, is decidedly erroneous; for during the first thirty years of the existence of that kingdom no such anarchic state of things existed as is portrayed in vv. 5 and 6, and still less could a return of the ten tribes to the Lord at that time be spoken of (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:4</reference>). It is more difficult to decide between the two other main views. The grounds which Vitr., Ramb., Berth. adduce in support of the reference to the times of the judges are not convincing; for the contents and form (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:4</reference>) do not prove that here something is asserted which has been confirmed by history, and still less is it manifest (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2Ch 15:5</reference>) that past times are pointed to. Whether the statement about the return to Jahve in the times of trouble (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:4</reference>) refers to the past or to the future, depends upon whether the past or future is spoken of in 2Ch 15:3. But the unquiet condition of things portrayed in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2Ch 15:5</reference> corresponds partly to various times in the period of the judges; and if, with Vitr., we compare the general characteristics of the religious condition of the times of the judges (Jdg 2:10.), we might certainly say that Israel in those times was without אמת אלהי, as it again and again forsook Jahve and served the Baals. And moreover, several examples of the oppression of Israel portrayed in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2Ch 15:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.6">2Ch 15:6</reference> may be adduced from the time of the judges. Yet the words in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.6">2Ch 15:6</reference>, even when their rhetorical character is taken into account, are too strong for the anarchic state of things during the period of the judges, and the internal struggles of that time (Jdg 12:1-6 and 2 Chron 20). And consequently, although Vitr. and Ramb. think that a reference to experiences already past, and oppressions already lived through, would have made a much deeper impression than pointing forward to future periods of oppression, yet Ramb. himself remarks, <hi type="italic">nihilominus tamen in saeculis Asae imperium antegressis vix ullum tempus post ingressum in terram Canaan et constitutam rempubl. Israel. posse ostendi, cui omnia criteria hujus orationis propheticae omni ex parte et secundum omnia pondera verbis insita conveniant</hi>. But, without doubt, the omission of any definite statement of the time in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference> is decisive against the exclusive reference of this speech to the past, and to the period of the judges. The verse contains no verb, so that the words may just as well refer to the past as to the future. The prophet has not stated the time definitely, because he was giving utterance to truths which have force at all times,<note placement="foot">As Ramb. therefore rightly remarks, “<hi type="italic">Vatem videri consulto abstinuisse a determinatione temporis, ut vela sensui quam amplissime panderentur, verbaque omnibus temporum periodis adplicari possent, in quibus criteria hic recensita adpareant</hi>.”</note> and which Israel had had experience of already in the time of the judges, but would have much deeper experience of in the future. <div eID="gen6021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> We must take the words in this general sense, and supply neither a preterite nor a future in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference>, neither <hi type="italic">fuerant</hi> nor <hi type="italic">erunt</hi>, but must express the first clause by the present in English: “Many days are for Israel (i.e., Israel lives many days) without the true God, and without teaching priests, and without law.” רבּים ימים is not accus. of time (Berth.), but the subject of the sentence; and אלה ללא is not subject - “during many days there was to the people Israel no true God” (Berth.), - but predicate, while ל expresses the condition into which anything comes, and לא forms part of the following noun: Days for Israel for having not a true God. ללא differs from בּלא, “without,” just as ל differs from בּ; the latter expressing the being in a condition, the former the coming into it. On אמת אלהי, cf. Jer 10:10. אמת כּהן is not to be limited to the high priest, for it refers to the priests in general, whose office it was to teach the people law and justice (<reference osisRef="Lev.10.10">Lev 10:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.33.10">Deu 33:10</reference>). The accent is upon the predicates אמת and אמת. Israel had indeed Elohim, but not the true God, and also priests, but not priests who attended to their office, who watched over the fulfilment of the law; and so they had no תּורה, notwithstanding the book of the law composed by Moses.
entries.3c63da6754b39d1a14f10189879d4c456b566a1d: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2Ch 15:5</reference> “And in these times is no peace to those going out or to those coming in.” Free peaceful intercommunication is interfered with (cf. Jdg 5:6; Jdg 6:2), but great terrors upon all inhabitants of the lands (הערצות are, according to the usage of the chronicler, the various districts of the land of Israel).
entries.72aef4a4b482699ef19cdf70d2072c1006e45190: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.6-2Chr.15.7">2Ch 15:6-7</reference> “And one people is dashed in pieces by the other, and one city by the other; for God confounds them by all manner of adversity.” המם denotes confusion, which God brings about in order to destroy His enemies (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.24">Exo 14:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.10.10">Jos 10:10</reference>; Jdg 4:15). Days when they were without the true God, without teaching prophets, and without law, Israel had already experienced in the times of defection after Joshua (cf. Jdg 2:11.), but will experience them in the future still oftener and more enduringly under the idolatrous kings in the Assyrian and Babylonian exile, and still even now in its dispersion among all nations. That this saying refers to the future is also suggested by the fact that Hosea (Hos 3:4) utters, with a manifest reference to <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.3">2Ch 15:3</reference> of our speech, a threat that the ten tribes will be brought into a similar condition (cf. Hos 9:3-4); and even Moses proclaimed to the people that the punishment of defection from the Lord would be dispersion among the heathen, where Israel would be compelled to serve idols of wood and stone (Deu 4:27., <reference osisRef="Deut.28.36">Deu 28:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.64">Deu 28:64</reference>), i.e., would be without the true God. That Israel would, in such oppression, turn to its God, would seek Him, and that the Lord would be found of them, is a thought also expressed by Moses, the truth of which Israel had not only had repeated experience of during the time of the judges, but also would again often experience in the future (cf. Hos 3:5; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.1">Jer 31:1</reference>; Eze 36:24.; Rom 11:25.). בּצּר־לו refers back to <reference osisRef="Deut.4.30">Deu 4:30</reference>; the expression in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.4">2Ch 15:4</reference> is founded upon <reference osisRef="Deut.4.29">Deu 4:29</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.55.6">Isa 55:6</reference>). - Of the oppression in the times of defection portrayed in 2Ch 15:5., Israel had also had in the time of the judges repeated experience (cf. Jdg 5:6), most of all under the Midianite yoke (Jdg 6:2); but such times often returned, as the employment of the very words of the first hemistich of <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.5">2Ch 15:5</reference> in Zec 8:10, in reference to the events of the post-exilic time, shows; and not only the prophet Amos (<reference osisRef="Amos.3.9">Amo 3:9</reference>) sees רבּות מהוּמות, great confusions, where all is in an indistinguishable whirl in the Samaria of his time, but they repeated themselves at all times when the defection prevailed, and godlessness degenerated into revolution and civil war. Azariah portrays the terrors of such times in strong colours (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.6">2Ch 15:6</reference>): “Dashed to pieces is people by people, and city by city.” The war of the tribes of Israel against Benjamin (Judg 20:f.), and the struggle of the Gileadites under Jephthah with Ephraim (Jdg 12:4.), were civil wars; but they were only mild preludes of the <hi type="italic">bellum omnium contra omnes</hi> depicted by Azariah, which only commenced with the dissolution of both kingdoms, and was announced by the later prophets as the beginning of the judgment upon rebellious Israel (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.9.17-Isa.9.20">Isa 9:17-20</reference>), and upon all peoples and kingdoms hostile to God (Zec 14:13; <reference osisRef="Matt.24.7">Mat 24:7</reference>). With הממם אלהים כּי cf. רבּה יי מהוּמת, Zec 14:13. To this portrayal of the dread results of defection from the Lord, Azariah adds (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.7">2Ch 15:7</reference>) the exhortation, “Be ye strong (vigorous), and show yourselves not slack, languid” (cf. Zep 3:16; <reference osisRef="Neh.6.9">Neh 6:9</reference>); i.e., in this connection, proceed courageously and vigorously to keep yourselves true to the Lord, to exterminate all idolatry; then you shall obtain a great reward: cf. on these words, Jer 31:16.
entries.db157d95fd50c6c102fd2fe16c3517b498f8ef58: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8-2Chr.15.9">2Ch 15:8-9</reference> <hi type="italic">Completion of the reform in worship, and the renewal of the covenant</hi>. - 2Ch 15:8. The speech and prophecy of the prophet strengthened the king to carry out the work he had begun, viz., the extirpation of idolatry from the whole land. In <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Ch 15:8</reference> the words הנּניא עדד are surprising, not only because the prophet is called in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1">2Ch 15:1</reference>, not Oded, but Azariah the son of Oded, but also on account of the preceding הנּבוּאה in the absolute state, which cannot stand, without more ado, for the stat. constr. נבוּאת (cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.29">2Ch 9:29</reference>). The view of Cler. and Ew., that by an orthographical error בּן עזריהוּ has been dropped out, does not remove the difficulty, for it leaves the stat. absol. הנּבוּאה .lo unexplained. This is also the case with the attempt to explain the name Oded in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Ch 15:8</reference> by transposing the words Azariah ben Oded, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.1">2Ch 15:1</reference>, so as to obtain Oded ben Azariah (Movers); and there seems to be no other solution of the difficulty than to strike out the words Oded the prophet from the text as a gloss which has crept into it (Berth.), or to suppose that there is a considerable hiatus in the text caused by the dropping out of the words בּן עזריהוּ דּבּר אשׁר.<note placement="foot">C. P. Caspari, <hi type="italic">der Syrisch-ephraimitische Krieg</hi>, Christian. 1849, S. 51, explains the <hi type="italic">absol</hi>. הנּבוּאה by an ellipse, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.14">Isa 3:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.11">Isa 8:11</reference>, “the prophecy (that) of Oded,” but answers the question why Oded is used in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.8">2Ch 15:8</reference> instead of Azarjahu ben Oded by various conjectures, none of which can be looked upon as probable.</note> התחזק corresponds to חזקוּ. Asa complied with the exhortation, and removed (ויּעבר, as in 1Ki 15:12) all abominations (idols) from the whole land, and from the cities which he had taken from Mount Ephraim: these are the cities which Asa’s father Abijah had conquered, 2Ch 13:19. “And he renewed the altar before the porch,” i.e., the altar of burnt-offering, which might stand in need of repairs sixty years after the building of the temple. The Vulg. is incorrect in translating dedicavit, and Berth. in supposing that the renovation refers only to a purification of it from defilement by idolatry. חדּשׁ is everywhere to renew, repair, <hi type="italic">restaurare</hi>; cf. 2Ch 24:4. - But in order to give internal stability to the reform he had begun, Asa prepared a great sacrificial festival, to which he invited the people out of all the kingdom, and induced them to renew the covenant with the Lord. 2Ch 15:9. He gathered together the whole of Judah and Benjamin, and the strangers out of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon, who dwelt among them. Strangers, i.e., Israelites from the ten tribes, had come over as early as Rehoboam’s reign to the kingdom of Judah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.16">2Ch 11:16</reference>); these immigrations increased under Asa when it was seen that Jahve was with him, and had given him a great victory over the Cushites. It is surprising that Simeon should be mentioned among the tribes from which Israelites went over to the kingdom of Judah, since Simeon had received his heritage in the southern district of the tribal domain of Judah, so that at the division of the kingdom it would not well separate itself from Judah, and join with the tribes who had revolted from the house of David. The grouping together of Simeon, Ephraim, and Manasseh, both in our verse and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.34.6">2Ch 34:6</reference>, can consequently scarcely be otherwise explained than by the supposition, either from the cities assigned to them under Joshua into districts in the northern kingdom (Berth.), or that the Simeonites, though politically united with Judah, yet in religious matters were not so, but abstained from taking part in the Jahve-worship in Jerusalem, and had set up in Beersheba a worship of their own similar to that in Bethel and Dan. In such a case, the more earnest and thoughtful people from Simeon, as well as from Ephraim and Manasseh, may have gone to Jerusalem to the sacrificial festival prepared by Asa. In favour of this last supposition we may adduce the fact that the prophet Amos, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.5">Amo 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.4.4">Amo 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.14">Amo 8:14</reference>, mentions Beersheba, along with Bethel and Gilgal, as a place to which pilgrimages were made by the idolatrous Israelites.
entries.966ff0900964e4f7dfccd7f95b66bcc3f741607b: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10-2Chr.15.11">2Ch 15:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen6022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> At this festival, which was held on the third month of the fifteenth year of Asa’s reign, they offered of the booty, i.e., of the cattle captured in the war against the Cushites (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14">2Ch 14:14</reference>), 700 oxen and 7000 sheep. הביאוּ מן־השּׁלל defines the ויּזבּחוּ more closely: they sacrificed, viz., from the booty they offered. From this it seems to follow that the sacrificial festival was held soon after the return from the war against the Cushites. The attack of the Cushite Zerah upon Judah can only have occurred in the eleventh year of Asa, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference>; but it is not stated how long the war lasted, nor when Asa returned to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.14">2Ch 14:14</reference>) after conquering the enemy and plundering the towns of the south land. But Asa may quite well have remained longer in the south after the Cushites had been driven back, in order again firmly to establish his rule there; and on his return to Jerusalem, in consequence of the exhortation of the prophet Azariah, may have straightway determined to hold a sacrificial festival at which the whole people should renew the covenant with the Lord, and have set apart and reserved a portion of the captured cattle for this purpose.
entries.8ad398ba07844351a8ec9f9e3c6a643950243def: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.12">2Ch 15:12</reference> <div eID="gen6023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6024" type="x-p"/> And they entered into the covenant, i.e., they renewed the covenant, bound themselves by a promise on oath (שׁבוּעה, <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.14">2Ch 15:14</reference>) to hold the covenant, viz., to worship Jahve the God of the fathers with their whole heart and soul; cf. Deu 4:29. With בּבּרית בּוא, cf. Jer 34:10.
entries.9d4618dea5d9e7332218c6c8161bc39f0dca3002: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.13-2Chr.15.14">2Ch 15:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen6024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6025" type="x-p"/> To attest the sincerity of their return to the Lord, they determined at the same time to punish defection from Jahve on the part of any one, without respect to age or sex, with death, according to the command in <reference osisRef="Deut.17.2">Deu 17:2</reference>-6. ליהוה דרשׁ לא, not to worship Jahve, is substantially the same as to serve other gods, Deu 17:3. This they swore aloud and solemnly, בּתרוּעה, with joyful shouting and the sound of trumpets and horns.
entries.efd2e820205edd2f7f941728e55720fbcde97c6f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.15-2Chr.15.18">2Ch 15:15-18</reference> <div eID="gen6025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6026" type="x-p"/> This return to the Lord brought joy to all Judah, i.e., to the whole kingdom, because they had sworn with all their heart, and sought the Lord בכל־רצונם, with perfect willingness and alacrity. Therefore Jahve was found of them, and gave them rest round about. - In <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16-2Chr.15.18">2Ch 15:16-18</reference>, in conclusion, everything which still remained to be said of Asa’s efforts to promote the Jahve-worship is gathered up. Even the queen-mother Maachah was deposed by him from the dignity of ruler because she had made herself an image of Asherah; yet he did not succeed in wholly removing the altars on the high places from the land, etc. These statements are also to be found in 1Ki 15:13-16, and are commented upon at that place. Only in the Chronicle we have אסא אם instead of אמּו (Kings), because there Maachah had just been named (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">2Ch 15:10</reference>); and to the statement as to the abolition of idolatry, ירק, crushed, is added, and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.17">2Ch 15:17</reference> מיּשׂראל; while, on the other hand, after שׁלם, יהוה עם is omitted, as not being necessary to the expression of the meaning.
entries.7a27a489aa03f2d7c1ea025d5c692480227094ee: <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Ch 15:19</reference> <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.19">2Ch 15:19</reference> is different from 1Ki 15:16. In the latter passage it is said: war was between Asa and Baasha the king of Israel כּל־ימיהם, i.e., so long as both reigned contemporaneously; while in the Chronicle it is said: war was not until the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign. This discrepancy is partly got rid of by taking מלחמה in the book of Kings to denote the latent hostility or inimical attitude of the two kingdoms towards each other, and in the Chronicle to denote a war openly declared. The date, until the thirty-fifth year, causes a greater difficulty; but this has been explained in <reference osisRef="2Chr.16.1">2Ch 16:1</reference> by the supposition that in the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s reign war broke out between Asa and Baasha, when the meaning of our 16th verse would be: It did not come to war with Baasha until the thirty-sixth year of Asa’s rule. For further remarks on this, see on 2Ch 16:1.  <chapter eID="2Chr.15"/> <div eID="gen6026" type="x-p"/>
